t: Path In Zigzag Labelled Binary Tree — Level Math & Mirror Mapping
o: The tree is a perfect binary tree whose rows alternate direction: odd rows (1st, 3rd, ...) are labelled left-to-right, even rows right-to-left. We must output the labels on the root-to-node path for a given label. For label = 14: row 1 is [1], row 2 is [3,2] (reversed), row 3 is [4,5,6,7], row 4 is [15,14,13,12,11,10,9,8]; the path to 14 is 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 14. For label = 26: row 5 spans [31..16] reversed, and walking up gives 1,2,6,10,26. Since label <= 10^6, the tree has at most ~20 levels, so an O(log n) walk from the node up to the root is trivially fast — no tree construction needed.
k: A node with label L in level d (0-indexed) has parent at level d-1; its 'normal' position in that level can be recovered by mirroring.
In a normal (non-zigzag) perfect tree, the parent of label L is floor(L/2).
Zigzag only permutes labels within each level, so we can convert to normal coordinates, take the parent, then convert back.

a.i: For a node at level d (root = level 0), the level spans values [2^d, 2^(d+1)-1]. If the row is reversed, map the label to its mirrored twin within the level: L' = 3*2^d - 1 - L. In normal coordinates the parent is L'/2. If the child's row was reversed, the parent's row has opposite parity, so we may need to mirror back — but doing the mirror consistently per level while walking up handles it automatically: compute parent in normal space, then if the parent's level is reversed, mirror it into zigzag coordinates. Repeat until reaching the root, then reverse the collected list.
s: Start with the given label; find its level d = floor(log2(label)).
Append the current label to the answer path.
If level d is even-indexed (d % 2 == 1 means reversed since root is level 0... i.e., reversed when d is odd), mirror: L = 3*2^d - 1 - L.
Set L = L // 2 (parent in normal coordinates); if the new level is reversed, mirror again before next iteration.
Repeat until L == 1, then reverse the path and return it.
a.t: O(log n) — one constant-time step per level, and there are at most ~20 levels for n <= 10^6.
a.sp: O(log n) — the result path stores one label per level.

a.n: Approach 2: Simpler upward walk with single mirror trick
a.i: A cleaner formulation avoids double-mirroring: first mirror the starting label into 'normal' coordinates if its level is reversed. From then on, repeatedly take parent = L/2 in normal coordinates, but emit the zigzag label of each ancestor by mirroring it whenever its own level is reversed. This separates 'navigation' (normal tree arithmetic) from 'output formatting' (per-level mirroring), which many find easier to reason about.
s: Compute level d of the label; if d is odd (reversed row), replace label with its mirror 3*2^d - 1 - label.
Walk up: at each level, compute the zigzag display value by mirroring if the current level is odd, else use the value directly; push it to the result.
Update value = value // 2 and decrement the level.
Stop after processing level 0 (value 1), then reverse the result.
a.t: O(log n) — one iteration per level of the tree.
a.sp: O(log n) — for the output path.

w: Prefer Approach 2 in an interview: separating navigation (parent = L/2 in normal coordinates) from presentation (mirror per level) is easiest to explain and verify. Key pitfalls: off-by-one in the mirror formula (for level d spanning [2^d, 2^(d+1)-1], the mirror of L is 2^d + 2^(d+1) - 1 - L), forgetting that the root's level is 0 so *odd* levels are reversed, and forgetting to reverse the collected path at the end. Edge cases: label = 1 returns [1]; label = 2 or 3 returns [1, x]. Follow-ups might ask for the downward path construction, handling a k-ary zigzag tree, or computing the path without building any structure — all solved by the same level-arithmetic ideas.
